name: Quantum Oppenheimer-Snyder Black Hole
description: Oppenheimer and Snyder's ball of dust with the bounce of loop quantum cosmology inside it, which Jerzy Lewandowski, Yongge Ma, Jinsong Yang, and Cong Zhang built in 2023. The dust falls, stops at a finite density, and comes back out, and the junction conditions fix the vacuum outside: Schwarzschild's metric with one more term, with two horizons above a least mass and none below it.
convention: The mass is the length $m = GM/c^2$, and the area $\alpha = 16\sqrt{3}\,\pi\gamma^3\ell_p^2$ sets the quantum correction, with $\gamma$ the Barbero-Immirzi parameter and $\ell_p = \sqrt{G\hbar/c^3}$ the Planck length. We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\lambda{}_{\mu\lambda\nu}$.
history: A ball of dust with nothing to hold it up falls in on itself, and in Einstein's theory its density becomes infinite at the centre after a finite time of its own [oppenheimersnyder1939]. J. Robert Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder solved that collapse exactly in 1939, matching a contracting piece of a dust universe onto Schwarzschild's vacuum outside it [oppenheimersnyder1939]. In loop quantum cosmology the universe run backwards never reaches a big bang: in the words of Abhay Ashtekar, Tomasz Pawlowski, and Parampreet Singh, "the big bang is replaced by a big bounce" [ashtekar2006bounce]. Its Friedmann equation carries one more factor, $$H^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho\left(1 - \frac{\rho}{\rho_c}\right),$$ so the density can never exceed a critical value $\rho_c$, of the order of the Planck density [lewandowski2023, kelly2021]. How does Oppenheimer and Snyder's ball fall when its inside is a small bouncing universe?¶At the University of New Brunswick in 2020, Jarod George Kelly, Robert Santacruz, and Edward Wilson-Ewing solved the effective equations of loop quantum gravity for a spherical vacuum exactly [kelly2020]. Far from the centre their solution is Schwarzschild's black hole, with a quantum correction that falls off as $r^{-4}$ [kelly2020]. Its curvature scalars stay below bounds set by the Planck scale, whatever the mass [kelly2020]. The solution holds only outside a least radius, $r_b = (\alpha m/2)^{1/3}$, as Rodolfo Gambini, Javier Olmedo, and Jorge Pullin had already pointed out, and Kelly, Santacruz, and Wilson-Ewing took it as "indicating the need for a matter field" inside [kelly2020, gambini2020]. The same three then made that matter Oppenheimer and Snyder's dust, and with the effects at its edge set aside, the dust obeys the bouncing Friedmann equation and its surface turns round at precisely $r_b$ [kelly2021].¶Jerzy Lewandowski, Yongge Ma, Jinsong Yang, and Cong Zhang put the question the other way round, taking the bouncing ball as given and asking what the outside must be [lewandowski2023]. They allowed any static, spherically symmetric outside, with two unknown functions in it, and glued it to the dust so that the metric and the extrinsic curvature agree on its surface [lewandowski2023]. The junction conditions fix both functions, $$ds^2 = -f\,c^2dt^2 + \frac{dr^2}{f} + r^2d\Omega^2, \qquad f = 1 - \frac{2m}{r} + \frac{\alpha m^2}{r^4},$$ with $\alpha = 16\sqrt{3}\,\pi\gamma^3\ell_p^2$, $\gamma$ the Barbero-Immirzi parameter and $\ell_p$ the Planck length [lewandowski2023]. In their words the metric is "a suitably deformed Schwarzschild one" [lewandowski2023]. It is Kelly, Santacruz, and Wilson-Ewing's vacuum again [lewandowski2023, kelly2020]. A static observer outside the ball would measure an energy density in the vacuum that falls off as $r^{-6}$, "a purely quantum effect", which they thought might bear on dark matter [lewandowski2023].¶Whether a black hole forms depends on the mass [lewandowski2023]. Below $m = 4\sqrt{\alpha}/3\sqrt{3}$, about a Planck mass, $f$ has no zero, and the ball falls to $r_b$, bounces, and comes back out with no horizon anywhere [lewandowski2023]. Above it there are two horizons, and the regions stack into a tower like Reissner and Nordström's [lewandowski2023]. The surface of the ball falls through the event horizon and then an inner horizon, turns round at $r_b$, and climbs out through a white hole into another asymptotically flat universe [lewandowski2023]. Someone who stays outside watches the ball sink behind the horizon and never sees the bounce, while someone in the next universe sees the white hole first and then "a ball of dust pouring out of it" [lewandowski2023]. The horizon of the white hole is also a Cauchy horizon, which they expected to be unstable, as Reissner and Nordström's is [lewandowski2023].¶Glued the other way, with the dust outside, the same construction gives a quantum Swiss cheese: an empty bubble in a bouncing universe, squeezed until a horizon forms unless the bubble is about a Planck length across [lewandowski2023]. Viqar Husain joined Kelly, Santacruz, and Wilson-Ewing in 2022 to follow the collapse numerically, and in their simulations "trapped surfaces form and disappear as an initially collapsing density profile evolves into an outgoing shockwave" [husain2022]. They found the lifetime of the hole growing as the square of its mass, and no mass inflation at the inner horizons [husain2022]. Alfio Bonanno, Daniele Malafarina, and Antonio Panassiti built the same kind of collapse in asymptotic safety, where the strength of gravity falls at high energy, and their dust never reaches zero size in any finite time [bonanno2024]. There too the junction conditions fix the outside, with two horizons, one, or none, depending on how strong the correction is [bonanno2024].

related.text: The classical collapse, whose dust falls to infinite density at its centre. With the bounce of loop quantum cosmology inside the ball, the junction conditions put Schwarzschild's metric with one more term outside it [lewandowski2023].
The outside at $\alpha = 0$, where the quantum correction is gone and $f = 1 - 2m/r$ with $r_s = 2m$.
The inside of the ball, a flat Friedmann universe of dust whose scale factor bounces at $a = 1$ by the Friedmann equation of loop quantum cosmology [lewandowski2023, kelly2021].

The same tower of regions, with two horizons and universe after universe above them. Reissner and Nordström's correction to Schwarzschild's $f$ falls off as $r^{-2}$, and this one's as $r^{-4}$ [kelly2020, lewandowski2023].
Another black hole with two horizons above a least mass and none below it, written down by Hayward as a minimal model [hayward2006].
A black hole with an outer and an inner horizon and a regular centre. Kelly, Santacruz, and Wilson-Ewing set the two horizons of their vacuum beside Bardeen's [kelly2020].
The growth of the mass at an inner horizon. Husain, Kelly, Santacruz, and Wilson-Ewing found none at the inner horizons of their quantum collapse of dust [husain2022].
The whole universe bouncing, filled with a massless scalar field, the setting where Ashtekar, Pawlowski, and Singh found the bouncing Friedmann equation [ashtekar2006improved].

coordinates.name: Static Exterior
domains: r = r_b = \left(\alpha m/2\right)^{1/3} \;\text{(where the surface of the dust turns round)}

parameters.description: Area that sets the quantum correction, $\alpha = 16\sqrt{3}\,\pi\gamma^3\ell_p^2$. The surface of the dust turns round at $r_b = (\alpha m/2)^{1/3}$, and there are two horizons for $m > 4\sqrt{\alpha}/3\sqrt{3}$, with $r_\pm$ their radii and $\kappa_\pm$ their surface gravities, one for $m = 4\sqrt{\alpha}/3\sqrt{3}$, and none below

coordinates.convention: We use Lewandowski, Ma, Yang, and Zhang's coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Painlevé-Gullstrand Exterior
domains: r = r_b = \left(\alpha m/2\right)^{1/3} \;\text{(where the surface of the dust turns round)}

parameters.description: Area that sets the quantum correction, $\alpha = 16\sqrt{3}\,\pi\gamma^3\ell_p^2$. The surface of the dust turns round at $r_b = (\alpha m/2)^{1/3}$, and there are two horizons for $m > 4\sqrt{\alpha}/3\sqrt{3}$, with $r_\pm$ their radii and $\kappa_\pm$ their surface gravities, one for $m = 4\sqrt{\alpha}/3\sqrt{3}$, and none below

coordinates.convention: We use Kelly, Santacruz, and Wilson-Ewing's coordinates $(\tau, r, \theta, \phi)$, whose $\tau$ carries dimensions of time and is the proper time of an observer falling from rest far away, and take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein Exterior
domains: r = r_b = \left(\alpha m/2\right)^{1/3} \;\text{(where the surface of the dust turns round)}

parameters.description: Area that sets the quantum correction, $\alpha = 16\sqrt{3}\,\pi\gamma^3\ell_p^2$. The surface of the dust turns round at $r_b = (\alpha m/2)^{1/3}$, and there are two horizons for $m > 4\sqrt{\alpha}/3\sqrt{3}$, with $r_\pm$ their radii and $\kappa_\pm$ their surface gravities, one for $m = 4\sqrt{\alpha}/3\sqrt{3}$, and none below

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - 2m/r + \alpha m^2/r^4\right)^{-1}$ and $r_* = 0$ at $r = r_b$.

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - 2m/r + \alpha m^2/r^4\right)^{-1}$ and $r_* = 0$ at $r = r_b$.

coordinates.name: Comoving Dust Interior

parameters.description: Scale factor of the dust, a pure number with $a = 1$ at the bounce, $a = \left(1 + 9c^2\tau^2/\alpha\right)^{1/3}$, which solves $\dot{a}^2 = 4\left(a^3 - 1\right)/\alpha a^4$
Comoving radius of the surface of the dust, a length fixed by the mass through $\chi_0^3 = \alpha m/2$

coordinates.convention: We use comoving coordinates $(\tau, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, where $\tau$ is the proper time of the dust, $\chi$ is the areal radius of a shell at the bounce, a length, and the ball is $\chi \le \chi_0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, a dot on the scale factor is $\dot{a} = \dfrac{1}{c}\dfrac{da}{d\tau}$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.
